transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-28
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Park (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (CTO, Osprey), Marcus Bell (Platform Eng), Elena Ortiz (Security), Samir Das (ML)

Summary (auto): Osprey is evaluating Redwood to power a PLG quickstart for their developer-facing API. Primary asks: fastest path to first token for devs, cost and latency tradeoffs, private connectivity options for regulated customers, and compliance artifacts.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining — can you hear me ok?
00:03 Priya Rao: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Maya.
00:06 Maya Chen: Great, I'm Maya, AE here at Redwood. With me is Liam, our systems engineer. We'll run through how folks typically get to first token, what free credits look like, and then dig into hosting choices.
00:18 Liam Park: Hi all. Quick note: I can show a short perf sketch if we want but first would love to understand your constraints — latency targets, any data residency or VPC needs.
00:29 Marcus Bell: Sure. For context, Osprey is building a dev-facing embedding/search product and we expect a PLG funnel. Initial target is TTFT under 30 minutes for a dev to make their first API call using our docs and the Redwood creds. But enterprise customers will require VPC peering and KMS.
00:45 Elena Ortiz: And we have SOC2 in the pipeline, so audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC matter. We also want to see encryption at rest and KMS integration for any dedicated or private deployments.
01:00 Maya Chen: Good. That's consistent with what we see. Our PLG flow for many customers: free credits seeded to accounts, a quickstart that hits the hosted Redwood API; TTFT is often minutes to get a token and a first call. If you need VPC or on-prem, that's the Private offering which does add onboarding time.
01:20 Priya Rao: Walk me through the time differences. Hosted quickstart sounds fast but what's the catch vs dedicated?
01:28 Liam Park: Hosted is basically self-serve — sign up, SDK, free credits, and you can make your first request within minutes. Dedicated is reserved capacity for production — that requires commitment and setup, maybe a few days to provision. Private (VPC/on-prem) can be multi-week because of networking and certs. Also, dedicated can give you predictable latency SLOs while hosted is bursty but we operate regional routing.
01:51 Samir Das: For our ML stack, token costs and latency matter. If I spin up embedding calls at scale, how much control do we have over batching and quantization?
02:02 Liam Park: Good question. We expose model profiles and batching knobs. Redwood Optimize will suggest batching and quantization for your workload; on Dedicated you can pin quantization profiles. On Hosted we have sane defaults and automatic batching but less low-level control.
02:17 Marcus Bell: Any support for prefix or KV cache for conversational workloads? We care about connected sessions.
02:24 Liam Park: Yes, KV cache is supported in the runtime — we do prefix caching and automatic cache reuse for identical contexts. Implementation differs: on Dedicated you get more control over cache sizing and eviction policies. Hosted caches are shared logical constructs with TTLs.
02:40 Elena Ortiz: On security, how does private compare? Can we bring our own KMS or HSM for encryption keys?
02:47 Maya Chen: For Private (VPC/on-prem) you can integrate your KMS/HSM. For Dedicated we support customer-managed keys through KMS integrations as well — it's a common request. Hosted supports server-side encryption and we have a managed KMS arrangement but not customer HSM in standard hosted plans.
03:05 Priya Rao: Ok. We also need audit logs that map API keys to org actions and retention. Is that standard?
03:12 Liam Park: Audit logs are available across offerings. Dedicated and Private get longer retention options and easier export to your SIEM. Hosted includes token-level cost breakdowns and request traces, but retention windows are shorter unless you purchase extended observability.
03:29 Priya Rao: For TTFT and PLG, what's the free credits model? Are they per-account, per-org?
03:36 Maya Chen: We usually seed developer accounts with free credits tied to the org signup. The standard PLG flow: developers sign up, are given starter credits, sample prompts in the docs, and a one-click SDK snippet. We also provide onboarding templates and a small demo app you can white-label.
03:51 Marcus Bell: Do those credits expire quickly? We want to run hackathons and extended trial periods for paid conversion.
03:57 Maya Chen: They are configurable. Out-of-the-box a 90-day expiry is common, but we can adjust for pilots. For enterprise pilots we often give a dedicated credit pool tied to an enterprise deal.
04:10 Samir Das: For our perf expectations — we're aiming 200ms median for generation at 256 tokens for model X (we may use a smaller open model). Any rough guidance?
04:20 Liam Park: 200ms median is achievable on Dedicated with pinned model variants and tuned kernels. On hosted, medians are often a bit higher due to multi-tenant variability, maybe 250–400ms depending on model size and region. We'll want to run a benchmark with your prompts and sequence lengths to set expectations.
04:39 Priya Rao: Can you do a bench run? We can share 50 sample prompts and an expected QPS pattern.
04:45 Liam Park: Absolutely. If you share prompts and histograms we'll schedule a bench run in our staging cluster, and output token-level latency and cost breakdown.
04:52 Elena Ortiz: About data retention for inference payloads — we need guaranteed non-retention for hosted flows for certain enterprise customers. Is that supported?
04:59 Maya Chen: Yes. We have contractual terms for non-retention in enterprise plans and can configure no-persist modes. For Private it's under your control. For Hosted, non-retention is available as an enterprise option.
05:12 Priya Rao: What's the pilot playbook? We want a path from PLG quickstart to a pilot with a handful of enterprise customers with VPC requirements.
05:20 Maya Chen: Typical path: 1) PLG self-serve onboarding with free credits to collect developer usage and early signals, 2) Run a 2–4 week pilot with dedicated capacity or hosted plus extended observability to monitor regressions, 3) For enterprise customers that require isolation, move to Dedicated or Private depending on networking. We can draft a 6–8 week runway.
05:42 Marcus Bell: Costs — can you ballpark unit token cost differences between hosted and dedicated?
05:48 Liam Park: Ballparks vary by model family, but dedicated can be 20–40% cheaper per-token at meaningful commit levels because you amortize GPU costs. Hosted gives flexibility and zero infra ops but higher marginal costs. We'll send a tailored estimate based on your traffic profile.
06:03 Samir Das: Any friction for SDKs or rate limits? We expect spikes from PLG signups.
06:09 Maya Chen: We have quotas and rate-limiting controls at token and request levels; you can tier by plan. For spikes, autoscaling on Dedicated or burst capacity options are available. Also, caching and batching recommendations can significantly reduce upstream load.
06:25 Priya Rao: For compliance — SSO, SCIM, role-based access — is that supported?
06:31 Liam Park: Yes, SAML/SSO and SCIM for user provisioning; RBAC is available across Dedicated and Private and for hosted with enterprise SSO.
06:40 Elena Ortiz: We need to see your SOC2 report and pen-test summary.
06:44 Maya Chen: We'll include SOC2 and a redacted penetration test summary in the security pack. I'll send the link after the call.
06:50 Priya Rao: What's the minimal friction path to get our devs to first token today?
06:54 Maya Chen: Self-serve hosted is the fastest — sign up, apply credits, use the SDK snippet. You can adapt our quickstart docs into your onboarding so your devs hit your product flow that calls Redwood under the hood. TTFT for a dev is typically under 30 minutes end-to-end if credentials and sample prompts are ready.
07:10 Marcus Bell: If we want to do a gated pilot for enterprise customers behind our VPC, how much lead time for Private?
07:17 Liam Park: Private is a heavier lift — networking, certs, k8s config if on-prem — usually 3–6 weeks depending on access. If you want something faster, Dedicated with VPC peering can be a mid-ground — usually a week or two.
07:32 Samir Das: You mentioned Redwood Optimize earlier — is that a separate product or part of platform?
07:36 Maya Chen: Redwood Optimize is part of the platform — it surfaces batching/caching/quantization recommendations and tracks unit-cost regressions. We can enable it in pilot to tune for your workload.
07:47 Priya Rao: Ok, can you give an example of a pilot success criteria?
07:51 Liam Park: Sure. Example pilot success: 1) 95th pctile latency < 800ms for embedding workloads on your sample traffic; 2) cost per 1k embeddings below $X (we'll draft); 3) enterprise customers able to connect via VPC and KMS integration; 4) no functional regressions over a 2-week eval with our eval harness.
08:12 Marcus Bell: On the migration path from Hosted to Dedicated, how transparent is model versioning and rollouts?
08:18 Liam Park: You can pin model versions and use rollout policies — canary, A/B, and automatic fallback. The same API surface works across Hosted/Dedicated/Private so your app code doesn't need big changes.
08:30 Priya Rao: Do you support function/tool calling or structured output? We use tool calls for enrichment.
08:36 Maya Chen: Yes, streaming and function-calling patterns are supported; structured output via JSON schema enforcement is available. We'll show examples in the quickstart repo.
08:45 Samir Das: Any gotchas we should know when running benchmarks?
08:48 Liam Park: Two things: warm-up and KV cache behavior — cold KV caches will skew latency. Also sequence length variance affects kernel selection; share realistic histograms and we'll account for that.
08:58 Priya Rao: Alright — sounds good. Let's agree next steps.
09:02 Maya Chen: To recap: Redwood will send tailored pricing, a security pack including SOC2, and schedule a performance bench run — SE-driven. Osprey will share 50 prompts and traffic distribution and confirm pilot customers who need VPC.
09:16 Priya Rao: Yes. We'll aim to get the prompts and histogram to you by 2027-03-01.
09:22 Elena Ortiz: I'll send the SOC2 questionnaire and list of compliance requirements by 2027-03-03.
09:28 Maya Chen: Great. Liam, can you own the bench run?
09:31 Liam Park: Yup, I'll schedule the bench, run with stage tokens and provide a latency/cost report within 72 hours of receiving the artifacts.
09:39 Samir Das: One more minor point — developer docs customization. Can we white-label quickstart snippets so they point to our sample app?
09:45 Maya Chen: Yes, we provide quickstart templates you can fork and customize. I'll include the GitHub link in the follow-up.
09:52 Priya Rao: Perfect. Anything else?
09:55 Maya Chen: Not from me. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the pack and pricing.
10:00 Meeting ends.
